interactions.label: Folate deficiency manifests clinically within months of dietary cessation, where

params.question: Folate deficiency manifests clinically within months of dietary cessation, whereas B12 deficiency takes years to become apparent. Which of the following best explains this difference in timeline?

answers.text: Folate is absorbed in the proximal jejunum, which is more vulnerable to mucosal damage than the terminal ileum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While folate is indeed absorbed in the proximal jejunum, susceptibility to mucosal damage does not explain the difference in onset after dietary cessation. The critical factor is the size of body stores, not the vulnerability of the absorption site.

answers.text: B12 body stores in the liver are sufficient for 3–5 years, while folate stores last only 3–4 months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The liver holds 3–5 mg of B12, sufficient for 3–5 years, whereas total body folate stores are only 3–4 mg, lasting just 3–4 months. This large difference in reserve capacity is the primary reason B12 deficiency takes years to manifest while folate deficiency appears within months.

answers.text: B12 is bound to transcobalamin II in the blood, which prevents its renal excretion unlike folate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While B12 is indeed transported by transcobalamin II, this binding protein facilitates tissue delivery rather than preventing excretion. The difference in clinical onset is explained by the vastly different store durations: 3–5 years for B12 versus 3–4 months for folate.

answers.text: Dietary folate must be converted to monoglutamate before absorption, limiting the rate of storage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Although folate conjugase does trim dietary polyglutamate chains to monoglutamate for absorption, this enzymatic step does not limit storage capacity. The key difference is simply that total body folate stores (3–4 months) are far smaller than B12 stores (3–5 years).

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the storage differences between B12 and folate. The liver holds 3–5 mg of B12 (lasting 3–5 years) versus only 3–4 mg of folate (lasting 3–4 months), which is why folate deficiency appears much sooner after dietary cessation.
Well done. The difference in body stores — B12's 3–5 year hepatic reserve versus folate's 3–4 month supply — is the primary reason B12 deficiency takes much longer to manifest clinically.

interactions.label: A patient has vitamin B12 deficiency but normal dietary folate intake. Despite a

params.question: A patient has vitamin B12 deficiency but normal dietary folate intake. Despite adequate folate, their cells fail to synthesise DNA. Which mechanism best explains this paradox?

answers.text: B12 deficiency causes increased renal excretion of active folate forms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. B12 deficiency does not increase folate excretion. The problem is intracellular: folate becomes trapped in an unusable form (5-methyl THF) because methionine synthase cannot convert it back to tetrahydrofolate without B12 as a cofactor.

answers.text: Without B12, methionine synthase cannot release tetrahydrofolate from 5-methyl THF, trapping folate in an unusable form

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This is the 'folate trap.' Methionine synthase requires methylcobalamin to convert 5-methyl THF to THF. Without B12, 5-methyl THF accumulates and cannot be recycled into the active folate forms needed for thymidine and purine synthesis. The cell is functionally folate-deficient despite adequate dietary intake.

answers.text: B12 deficiency impairs dihydrofolate reductase, blocking the activation of dietary folate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Dihydrofolate reductase converts dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and does not require B12. The actual mechanism is the folate trap: without B12, methionine synthase cannot demethylate 5-methyl THF, so active folate forms become unavailable for DNA synthesis.

answers.text: B12 is required for folate absorption in the proximal jejunum, so its absence causes secondary folate malabsorption

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Folate absorption in the proximal jejunum does not require B12. The two vitamins have entirely separate absorption pathways. The link between them is intracellular: methionine synthase needs B12 to release usable tetrahydrofolate from 5-methyl THF.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the folate trap. Without B12, methionine synthase cannot convert 5-methyl THF to THF. Folate accumulates in an unusable methylated form, and the cell cannot produce the thymidine and purines needed for DNA synthesis.
Excellent. The folate trap is the central biochemical link between B12 and folate metabolism — B12 deficiency functionally starves cells of usable folate even when dietary intake is adequate.

interactions.label: Administering folate to a patient with undiagnosed vitamin B12 deficiency will c

params.question: Administering folate to a patient with undiagnosed vitamin B12 deficiency will correct the anaemia and also prevent further neurological damage.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. While folate does correct the anaemia (haemoglobin rises, the blood film normalises), it cannot prevent neurological damage. B12 is specifically required for S-adenosylmethionine synthesis, which maintains myelin integrity in the posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts. Giving folate alone masks the anaemia while spinal cord degeneration progresses unchecked — this is precisely why B12 deficiency must be excluded before treating with folate alone.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Folate supplementation does improve the haematological picture — haemoglobin rises and the blood film normalises. However, folate cannot substitute for B12 in the S-adenosylmethionine pathway that methylates myelin lipids. Subacute combined degeneration of the posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts continues silently, with the corrected anaemia removing the only clinical warning sign. This is one of haematology's most dangerous treatment errors.

interactions.label: A 45-year-old man presents with an MCV of 110 fL. His peripheral blood smear sho

params.question: A 45-year-old man presents with an MCV of 110 fL. His peripheral blood smear shows round macrocytes with target cells, but neutrophil segmentation is normal. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. B12 deficiency produces megaloblastic macrocytosis with distinctly oval macrocytes (macro-ovalocytes) and hypersegmented neutrophils. The round macrocytes and normal neutrophil segmentation in this patient rule out a megaloblastic cause.

Incorrect. Folate deficiency also causes megaloblastic macrocytosis — identical morphology to B12 deficiency — with oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. This patient's round macrocytes and normal neutrophils indicate a non-megaloblastic cause.

Correct. Round macrocytes, target cells, and normal neutrophil segmentation point to a non-megaloblastic cause. Liver disease loads excess cholesterol into the red cell membrane, producing round macrocytes and target cells. The absence of hypersegmented neutrophils is the key finding that rules out megaloblastic disease and confirms a non-megaloblastic aetiology.

Incorrect. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking DNA synthesis — this produces megaloblastic macrocytosis with oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. The normal neutrophil segmentation and round macrocytes here indicate a non-megaloblastic cause instead.

overallFeedback.feedback: Focus on the neutrophil. Hypersegmented neutrophils confirm megaloblastic disease; their absence sends you down the non-megaloblastic pathway. Round macrocytes with target cells and normal neutrophils are the signature of liver disease, which loads cholesterol into the red cell membrane.

Excellent. You correctly identified the non-megaloblastic pattern: round macrocytes, target cells, and normal neutrophils point to liver disease. The hypersegmented neutrophil is the pivotal finding that separates the two categories.

params.question: In a patient with confirmed megaloblastic anaemia, serum B12 is 250 pg/mL (equivocal range: 200–300 pg/mL). Which investigation should be performed next to clarify whether B12 deficiency is present?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Bone marrow biopsy is rarely needed for diagnosis in current practice. When serum B12 falls in the equivocal range, metabolite assays — methylmalonic acid and homocysteine — can resolve the ambiguity non-invasively and more specifically.

Incorrect. Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are used to identify pernicious anaemia as the cause of B12 deficiency, but they are ordered after B12 deficiency has been confirmed. They cannot determine whether B12 deficiency itself is present when the serum level is equivocal.

Correct. When serum B12 falls in the equivocal range (200–300 pg/mL), methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are the essential second-line investigations. Raised MMA plus raised homocysteine confirms B12 deficiency; raised homocysteine alone with normal MMA points to folate deficiency instead.

Incorrect. Red cell folate reflects three months of folate status and is useful for assessing folate deficiency, but it does not help clarify an equivocal B12 level. Methylmalonic acid — specific to B12 deficiency — is the metabolite that resolves the diagnostic ambiguity.

overallFeedback.feedback: When B12 levels are equivocal (200–300 pg/mL), the next step is to measure methylmalonic acid and homocysteine. MMA rises specifically in B12 deficiency, not in folate deficiency, and resolves the diagnostic ambiguity without the need for invasive testing.
Correct. When serum B12 is in the grey zone (200–300 pg/mL), MMA and homocysteine are the essential second-line assays that confirm or exclude B12 deficiency with far greater specificity.
